name: libnova
desc: Celestial mechanics, astrometry and astrodynamics library
why: A celestial mechanics and astrodynamics library that lets you compute orbits and positions, real astronomy at home.

brief.what_it_is: libnova is a general-purpose, double-precision C/C++ library for celestial mechanics, astrometry and astrodynamics. You call its functions with dates, times and orbital or coordinate inputs, and it returns computed values such as positions, apparent places, sidereal time, rise/set/transit times, magnitudes, semidiameters and orbit velocities. The page lists solar, planetary, lunar, asteroid and comet calculations, plus elliptic, parabolic and hyperbolic motion. It is the calculation engine behind the Nova project. The homepage does not describe a command-line tool beyond the libnovaconfig executable named in the Homebrew metadata, which the page does not mention.
brief.why_it_exists: The page says the intended audience is C/C++ programmers, astronomers, and anyone interested in calculating positions of astronomical objects or celestial mechanics, and that it is free software. Its algorithms come largely from Jean Meeus's Astronomical Algorithms, with the ELP 2000-82B lunar solution and the VSOP87 planetary solution credited.
brief.how_it_works: The homepage does not explain the internal mechanism beyond naming the published algorithms and series it implements (Meeus, ELP82 for the Moon, VSOP87 for the planets). It is a C library, so you link it into your own program and call its functions.
brief.install_notes: The homepage gives no build or install steps and no runtime or configuration requirements. It offers a source download, a git repository, and an offline API documentation tarball. The Homebrew metadata lists an executable called libnovaconfig, which is presumably a pkg-config style helper for compiler flags, but the page does not say so and I did not see its usage.
brief.standout: It is a long-lived, double-precision C library that puts classic published astronomy algorithms (Meeus, ELP82, VSOP87) behind one API, covering planets, Moon, asteroids, comets and rise/set times. It is LGPL-licensed, so you can link it from proprietary code.
brief.status: Looks quiet. The page was generated on Tue Mar 3 2015, the download section names 0.15.0 as the latest release, and the header says v 0.16.0. Those two version numbers disagree, which suggests the site has not been updated in a while. I did not check a release date or the git log, so this is an inference from the page, not a confirmed status.
brief.caveats: The page is a generated Doxygen-style API page from 2015 and is sparse on examples and usage. The version numbers conflict (header v 0.16.0, download 0.15.0). The site asks for help with documentation for novice users and with algorithm work, which suggests thin maintainer capacity. The homepage was reachable, but the git and download links were not followed, so I did not check whether the code has changed since 2015.
